pos: n. (Robert Barnes, c. 1495–1540, Augustinian prior of Cambridge, of the White Horse circle, who recanted in 1526, returned to the faith, and was burned at Smithfield under the Six Articles)
etymology: English Barnes, from the barns, a place-name surname; also written Barns and Bernes.
biblical_def: Robert Barnes was prior of the Augustinian house at Cambridge and one of the men who met at the White Horse Inn to read Luther and the Greek New Testament. Arrested in 1526 for a sermon against the pomp of the clergy, he was brought before Wolsey, carried a faggot in penance and abjured; he escaped abroad, reached Wittenberg, lodged with Luther and Bugenhagen, and became a useful envoy between the German churches and Thomas Cromwell. He returned under Cromwell's protection, served on embassies, and when Cromwell fell in 1540 Barnes fell with him — condemned by act of Parliament without trial and burned at Smithfield on 30 July, protesting at the stake that he did not know why he was dying. He is the man who drew back once and did not draw back twice. Heb 10:39 is his verse — “But we are not of them who draw back unto perdition; but of them that believe to the saving of the soul” — with 2Ti 1:8, “Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord,” and Rev 12:11, of those who “loved not their lives unto the death.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines to abjure as to renounce upon oath; to abandon; and to recant as to retract; to contradict a former declaration.
webster_full: ABJU'RE, v.t. To renounce upon oath; to abandon.
2. To retract, recant, or abjure a declaration or opinion.
RECANT', v.t. To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration.
scriptures: But we are not of them who draw back unto perdition; but of them that believe to the saving of the soul.
Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me his prisoner: but be thou partaker of the afflictions of the gospel according to the power of God;
And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony; and they loved not their lives unto the death.
Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints.
corruption_summary: Barnes abjured at thirty and burned at forty-five, and the second fact is the one the doctrine of perseverance predicts.
corruption_paragraphs: A recantation is a grievous fall and not necessarily a final one. Perseverance of the saints does not mean that the regenerate never fail under pressure; it means that God preserves His own so that they are brought back and kept to the end. Barnes carried his faggot in 1526 and walked to the fire in 1540, and the shape of that life is the shape Heb 10:39 describes — not of them who draw back unto perdition. The doctrine is misread when it is used to deny that a true believer can fall badly, and misread again when a bad fall is taken as proof that he never believed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the difference between a fall and an apostasy, and the patience it requires of a church. Barnes was received back by men who had seen him abjure. Psa 116:15 says “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints,” and it is said of a man whose record was not unbroken. The practical corollary is that a church must know how to restore the lapsed rather than only how to admire the steadfast.

roots_lines: Greek hupostole (G5289) — a drawing back, a shrinking; Hebrews 10:39.
Greek apoleia (G684) — perdition, destruction; Hebrews 10:39.
Greek epaischunomai (G1870) — to be ashamed of; 2 Timothy 1:8.
Greek marturia (G3141) — testimony, witness; Revelation 12:11.
Hebrew yaqar (H3368) — precious, costly; Psalm 116:15.

“Be not thou therefore ashamed of the testimony of our Lord” (2Ti 1:8) — after one abjuration.
“they loved not their lives unto the death” (Rev 12:11) — Smithfield, 1540.

pos: n. (John Lambert, d. 1538, English priest burned at Smithfield after disputing on the Lord's Supper before Henry VIII in person, whose last word was “None but Christ”)
etymology: English Lambert, from Germanic Landberht, land-bright; his family name was Nicholson.
biblical_def: John Lambert was a Cambridge man, chaplain to the English merchants at Antwerp, and twice examined for heresy before the case that killed him. In November 1538 he was brought to Westminster to dispute the bodily presence of Christ in the sacrament, and Henry VIII himself presided, seated in white silk, with Cranmer and Gardiner among the examiners; the king pressed him personally and ten bishops argued against him in succession through the afternoon. Asked at the end whether he would live or die, he committed his soul to God and his body to the king's clemency, and was burned four days later. The accounts say he lifted his hands out of the fire crying “None but Christ, none but Christ.” The doctrine he died for is Heb 10:12, that this man “after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God,” and 1Co 11:24, “this do in remembrance of me.” Joh 6:63 is the verse the Reformers pressed against a carnal eating: “It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines transubstantiation as the change of the bread and wine in the eucharist into the body and blood of Christ; a conversion maintained by the Romish church.
webster_full: TRANSUBSTANTIA'TION, n. The change of the bread and wine in the eucharist into the body and blood of Christ; a conversion which the Romish church maintains to be effected by the consecration.
EU'CHARIST, n. The sacrament of the Lord's supper; the solemn act of ceremony of commemorating the death of Christ.
COMMEM'ORATE, v.t. To call to remembrance by a solemn act.
scriptures: But this man, after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God;
And when he had given thanks, he brake it, and said, Take, eat: this is my body, which is broken for you: this do in remembrance of me.
Joh 6:63
It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.
And as they were eating, Jesus took bread, and blessed it, and brake it, and gave it to the disciples, and said, Take, eat; this is my body.
corruption_summary: A king sat in judgment on the Lord's Supper and a priest was burned for the answer, which is what happens when a sacrament is made a test of loyalty.
corruption_paragraphs: Transubstantiation is the error Lambert died denying, and the Reformed objection is not squeamishness about mystery but Heb 10:12 and Heb 10:14: Christ offered one sacrifice, for ever, and sat down. A rite that re-presents that offering daily contradicts the finished work, and a doctrine that locates Christ's body bodily on ten thousand altars contradicts the ascension. 1Co 11:26 fixes the sense of the ordinance: “as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come” — a showing forth until a coming, which presumes He is not bodily here.

Two further errors must be refused in the same breath, and the Reformed position is not a middle muddle but a definite doctrine. Rome's transubstantiation and the Lutheran sacramental union both place Christ's body in or under the elements; bare memorialism empties the sacrament of Christ altogether. Scripture gives a real spiritual presence received by faith, so that the believer truly feeds on Christ while the bread remains bread. Joh 6:63 is the hinge, and the Supper is a means of grace precisely because the Spirit quickens and the flesh profiteth nothing.

roots_lines: Greek anamnesis (G364) — a remembrance, a calling to mind; 1 Corinthians 11:24.
Greek soma (G4983) — a body; 1 Corinthians 11:24, Matthew 26:26.

Greek ephapax (G2178) — once for all; Hebrews 10:10 and the sense of 10:12.
Greek eulogeo (G2127) — to bless; Matthew 26:26.

“this do in remembrance of me” (1Co 11:24) — the ordinance's own account of itself.
“It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing” (Joh 6:63) — against a carnal eating.

pos: n. (Anne Askew, c. 1521–1546, Lincolnshire gentlewoman, racked in the Tower of London to make her name other women and burned at Smithfield)
etymology: English Askew, from Aiskew in Yorkshire; also written Ascue and Kyme, her married name.
biblical_def: Anne Askew was turned out by her husband for reading the Scriptures, went to London, and was arrested for denying that the bread of the sacrament is the body of Christ. Her Examinations, smuggled out and printed by John Bale, record her answers: pressed to interpret a text, she replied that she would not cast pearls among swine; asked whether a mouse eating the host had received God, she declined the question and asked them to answer it. Because her examiners wanted the names of ladies at court who shared her faith, she was taken to the Tower and racked — illegally, and in the end by the Lord Chancellor's own hands when the lieutenant refused. She named no one. Her joints were so broken that she was carried to Smithfield in a chair and burned sitting, aged about twenty-five. Heb 11:35 is written of such people: “others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection.” 1Co 1:27 names God's method, choosing “the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the rack as an engine of torture, used to extort confessions from criminals; and to torture as to pain to extremity; to put to the rack.
webster_full: RACK, n. An engine of torture, used to extort confessions from the accused or suspected.
2. Torture; extreme pain; anguish.
TOR'TURE, n. Extreme pain; anguish of body or mind; pang; agony; torment.
scriptures: Women received their dead raised to life again: and others were tortured, not accepting deliverance; that they might obtain a better resurrection:
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
But when they deliver you up, take no thought how or what ye shall speak: for it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak.
Psa 27:1
A Psalm of David. The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? the LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?
corruption_summary: A woman of twenty-five was racked to make her name her friends and did not, and her Examinations are the record she left instead.
corruption_paragraphs: Askew's examinations show something the martyrologies often flatten: she was not simply brave but shrewd, and she handled her interrogators with the discretion Christ commends. Mat 10:19 promises that “it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak,” and the promise is not of eloquence but of the right words, which sometimes means declining to answer a trap. The torture had a purpose beyond cruelty — the council wanted the Queen's ladies — and her silence protected women who would otherwise have burned with her.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the honour due to such a witness without turning her into a symbol of something else. Askew is sometimes enlisted as a proto-feminist heroine and her theology treated as incidental, which inverts her own account: she died over the doctrine of the sacrament, having been taught it from the English Bible she was thrown out of her house for reading. 1Co 1:27 is the right frame — God chose the weak thing to confound the mighty — and Psa 27:1 the confidence she acted on: “The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?”
roots_summary: Greek tumpanizo (G5178), to torture, to beat on a drum-frame; asthenes (G772), weak; Hebrew yesha (H3468), salvation.
roots_lines: Greek tumpanizo (G5178) — to torture on a frame; Hebrews 11:35.
Greek apolutrosis (G629) — deliverance, release; Hebrews 11:35.
Greek asthenes (G772) — weak, feeble; 1 Corinthians 1:27.
Greek kataischuno (G2617) — to confound, to put to shame; 1 Corinthians 1:27.
Hebrew maoz (H4581) — strength, a stronghold; Psalm 27:1.
usage: “others were tortured, not accepting deliverance” (Heb 11:35) — written of such people.
“God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27) — His method.
“it shall be given you in that same hour what ye shall speak” (Mat 10:19) — including what not to say.

pos: n. (John Rogers, c. 1500–1555, editor of Matthew's Bible of 1537 and the first martyr of Mary's reign, burned at Smithfield on 4 February 1555)
etymology: English Rogers, son of Roger, from Germanic Hrodgar, famous spear; he published his Bible under the pseudonym Thomas Matthew.
biblical_def: John Rogers was chaplain to the English merchants at Antwerp, where he met William Tyndale and was converted to the Reformed faith. After Tyndale's death he took the completed work — Tyndale's New Testament and his Old Testament through Chronicles, with Coverdale for the rest — added prefaces, marginal notes and the apocrypha, and published it in 1537 under the name Thomas Matthew. That volume, Matthew's Bible, was the first English Bible printed with royal licence, and so the first lawful English Scripture in English hands. He returned under Edward, held a prebend at St Paul's, preached against the old religion at Paul's Cross after Mary's accession, and was the first of her reign to burn. His wife and eleven children, one at the breast, met him on the way to Smithfield. 2Ti 2:9 is his monument: “I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.” Mat 5:10 is the beatitude, and Rev 6:9 shows under the altar “the souls of them that were slain for the word of God.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a version as a translation; and a martyr as one who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel.
webster_full: VER'SION, n. A translation; that which is rendered from another language.
M'ARTYR, n. One who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel.
PREF'ACE, n. Something spoken as introductory to a discourse, or written as introductory to a book.
scriptures: Wherein I suffer trouble, as an evil doer, even unto bonds; but the word of God is not bound.
Mat 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
Rev 6:9
And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar the souls of them that were slain for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held:
Psa 56:4
In God I will praise his word, in God I have put my trust; I will not fear what flesh can do unto me.
corruption_summary: The man who gave England its first licensed Bible was the first Englishman burned for believing it, and the two facts belong in one sentence.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew's Bible is the hinge of the English Scripture: Tyndale's work, saved and completed by Rogers, licensed in 1537, and the direct ancestor through the Great Bible and the Bishops' Bible of the Authorized Version of 1611. Much of what an English reader hears as the sound of Scripture is Tyndale's English preserved by Rogers's editing. That the editor was burned eighteen years later, under a queen restoring the religion that had killed Tyndale, is the plainest possible comment on who wanted the book suppressed. 2Ti 2:9 was proved twice over: the men were bound and the word was not.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the cost of the Bible an English household now owns cheaply. Rogers put his name to nothing — he used a pseudonym to protect the project — and died for the contents. Rev 6:9 locates such men under the altar, slain “for the word of God, and for the testimony which they held,” and the proper use of that knowledge is not sentiment but reading. Psa 56:4 is the steadiness he had: “In God I will praise his word, in God I have put my trust; I will not fear what flesh can do unto me.”
roots_summary: Greek deo (G1210), to bind; dioko (G1377), to persecute; sphazo (G4969), to slay.
roots_lines: Greek kakopathe'o (G2553) — to suffer trouble, to endure hardship; 2 Timothy 2:9.
Greek deo (G1210) — to bind; 2 Timothy 2:9.
Greek dioko (G1377) — to pursue, to persecute; Matthew 5:10.
Greek sphazo (G4969) — to slay, to butcher; Revelation 6:9.
Greek thusiasterion (G2379) — an altar; Revelation 6:9.

“Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake” (Mat 5:10) — the beatitude.
“the souls of them that were slain for the word of God” (Rev 6:9) — where such men are.

pos: n. (Laurence Saunders, d. 1555, rector of All Hallows, Bread Street, burned at Coventry on 8 February 1555, the second martyr of Mary's reign)
etymology: English Saunders, a form of Alexander's son; Laurence, from Latin Laurentius, of Laurentum.
biblical_def: Laurence Saunders gave up the study of law for divinity, was ordained under Edward, and preached in London and Northampton. When Mary's proclamation forbade preaching without licence he went on preaching, was arrested in his own pulpit at Bread Street, and spent fifteen months in the Marshalsea writing letters to his congregation and to his wife that Foxe preserved. Degraded and sent to Coventry, he was led out on 8 February 1555; the accounts say he took the stake in his arms and kissed it, saying “Welcome the cross of Christ, welcome everlasting life.” Gal 6:14 is the sentence behind that gesture: “God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.” 1Pe 4:13 is the command he obeyed, to “rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings,” and Rom 8:18 the reckoning he had made: “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the cross, figuratively, as the sufferings of Christ; also, anything that thwarts or opposes; affliction, trial, vexation.
webster_full: CROSS, n. A gibbet consisting of two pieces of timber placed across each other.
4. The ensign of the christian religion; and hence figuratively, the religion itself.
6. Anything that thwarts, obstructs or perplexes; hindrance; vexation; misfortune; opposition; trial of patience.
scriptures: Gal 6:14
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world.
But rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings; that, when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy.
Col 1:24
Who now rejoice in my sufferings for you, and fill up that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh for his body's sake, which is the church:
Rom 8:18
For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed in us.
corruption_summary: Saunders embraced the stake, and the sentence he said at it is the only kind of cross-talk the New Testament will support.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern devotional use of the cross has largely become figurative and small — a difficulty, an inconvenience, a burden one carries. Saunders used the word of a literal stake. The New Testament's own usage runs the other way from ours: Gal 6:14 glories in the cross of Christ as the thing by which the world is crucified to the believer, and 1Pe 4:13 speaks of partaking in sufferings that were actual. Where the word is softened, the comfort attached to it softens too, and a church that has only metaphorical crosses will have no vocabulary ready when real ones come.

Col 1:24 needs a word of care, since Rome has used it to support a treasury of merit: Paul rejoices to “fill up that which is behind of the afflictions of Christ in my flesh for his body's sake.” The afflictions in view are the sufferings that still fall on Christ's body in the world, not a deficiency in His atoning work, which Heb 10:14 declares perfect and complete. The recovery is both halves held: the atonement finished and unrepeatable, and the believer genuinely called to suffer with Him, with Rom 8:18 as the arithmetic that makes it bearable.

roots_lines: Greek stauros (G4716) — a cross, a stake; Galatians 6:14.
Greek kauchaomai (G2744) — to boast, to glory; Galatians 6:14.

pos: n. (Rowland Taylor, d. 1555, rector of Hadleigh in Suffolk, burned on Aldham Common within sight of his own parish on 9 February 1555)
etymology: English Taylor, an occupational surname, a cutter of cloth; Rowland, from Germanic Hrodland, famous land.
biblical_def: Rowland Taylor had been chaplain to Cranmer and held the rectory of Hadleigh, where he was known for feeding the poor of the parish out of his own tithes and for knowing every household. When Mary's commission came to say mass in his church he stood in the chancel and forbade it, and was summoned to London. Offered escape by friends, he refused to leave his people. He was condemned, taken back to Suffolk to die where his parishioners could watch, and burned on Aldham Common; Foxe records that the people of Hadleigh lined the road weeping and that he told them he was going to his own house. Joh 10:11 is the text the scene enacts: “I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.” 1Pe 5:3 is the manner of his ministry, “Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock,” and 2Co 12:15 the disposition, “I will very gladly spend and be spent for you.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pastor as a minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation; and a flock as a company or collection of Christians, the church.
webster_full: P'ASTOR, n. A shepherd; one that has the care of flocks and herds.
2. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation, whose duty is to watch over the people of his charge, and instruct them in the sacred doctrines of the christian religion.
FLOCK, n. In Scripture, a company or collection of Christians; the church.
scriptures: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock.
And I will very gladly spend and be spent for you; though the more abundantly I love you, the less I be loved.
Php 2:17
Yea, and if I be offered upon the sacrifice and service of your faith, I joy, and rejoice with you all.
corruption_summary: Taylor was offered a safe exile and would not leave his parish, which is the test the pastoral office is built to fail or pass.
corruption_paragraphs: The refusal to flee is not a universal rule — Paul left cities, and Christ withdrew more than once — but Joh 10:11 draws a line the hireling cannot cross: the good shepherd gives his life for the sheep, and the hireling flees because the sheep are not his own. Taylor had been given a charge, the wolves were at it, and he judged that leaving would preach a louder sermon than staying. The modern analogue is less dramatic and still real: a ministry treated as a career, moved for advantage, with the congregation a stage rather than a charge.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the pastor's identification with a particular people. 1Pe 5:3 forbids lording and requires example, and 2Co 12:15 describes an affection that spends itself without being repaid in kind — “though the more abundantly I love you, the less I be loved.” Php 2:17 is the disposition that makes such a ministry possible, a man content to be poured out on the sacrifice and service of other people's faith. Hadleigh had such a rector for eleven years and watched him burn.
roots_summary: Greek poimen (G4166), a shepherd; kleros (G2819), a lot, a heritage; ekdapanao (G1550), to spend out utterly.
roots_lines: Greek poimen (G4166) — a shepherd, a pastor; John 10:11.
Greek psuche (G5590) — life, soul; John 10:11.
Greek katakurieuo (G2634) — to lord it over; 1 Peter 5:3.
Greek ekdapanao (G1550) — to spend out utterly, to exhaust; 2 Corinthians 12:15.
Greek spendo (G4689) — to be poured out as a drink offering; Philippians 2:17.
usage: “the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (Joh 10:11) — the text Aldham Common enacted.
“Neither as being lords over God's heritage, but being ensamples to the flock” (1Pe 5:3) — the manner of his ministry.
“I will very gladly spend and be spent for you” (2Co 12:15) — the disposition it requires.

pos: n. (John Philpot, c. 1516–1555, Archdeacon of Winchester, examined fourteen times under Mary and burned at Smithfield on 18 December 1555)
etymology: English Philpot, a diminutive of Philip; also written Philpott.
biblical_def: John Philpot was a gentleman's son of Hampshire, a good Hebraist, and Archdeacon of Winchester under Edward. In the Convocation of 1553 he spoke against the restoration of the mass to its face and was imprisoned for it, and he spent eighteen months being examined — fourteen separate hearings before Bonner, Gardiner and others — of which he wrote his own detailed accounts and smuggled them out. They are among the most valuable documents of the English Reformation, because they show the arguments actually used on both sides rather than the martyrologist's summary. He was learned, quick and sometimes sharp to the point of rudeness with his examiners. Burned at Smithfield in December 1555, he is said to have kissed the stake and called it his school. Luk 21:15 is the promise he relied on: “For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.” Act 6:10 records it fulfilled in Stephen, and Psa 119:46 states the duty: “I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an examination as a careful search or inquiry; an interrogation; and to gainsay as to contradict; to oppose in words; to deny or declare not to be true.
webster_full: EXAMINA'TION, n. The act of examining; a careful search or inquiry, with a view to discover truth.
3. In judicial proceedings, a careful inquiry into facts by testimony.
GAINSAY', v.t. To contradict; to oppose in words; to deny or declare not to be true.
scriptures: For I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist.
Act 6:10
And they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake.
And ye shall be brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them and the Gentiles.
I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed.
corruption_summary: Philpot wrote down what his examiners actually said, and that is why his Examinations are worth more than a hundred pages of praise for him.
corruption_paragraphs: Martyrologies tend to give the martyr's courage and omit the argument, which quietly suggests that the issue was temperament rather than truth. Philpot's records do the opposite: they set out the Roman case on the sacrament, the church and tradition in his opponents' own words, with his replies, so a reader can judge. Mat 10:18 says believers will be “brought before governors and kings for my sake, for a testimony against them,” and a testimony is content, not merely bearing. The documents are a service to the church precisely because they are not hagiography.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that Luk 21:15 promises wisdom rather than exemption. The verse is sometimes read as a guarantee of deliverance, and Philpot's case shows what it actually gives: his adversaries could not gainsay nor resist him, and they burned him anyway. The promise is that the witness will be adequate, not that it will be accepted, and the Christian under examination may therefore prepare his answer and leave the outcome where Psa 119:46 leaves it, speaking before kings and not being ashamed.

roots_lines: Greek stoma (G4750) — a mouth, hence utterance; Luke 21:15.
Greek antepo and antilego (G483) — to speak against, to gainsay; Luke 21:15.
Greek anthistemi (G436) — to set against, to resist; Luke 21:15, Acts 6:10.
Greek marturion (G3142) — a testimony; Matthew 10:18.
Hebrew eduth (H5715) — testimonies; Psalm 119:46.
usage: “I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to gainsay nor resist” (Luk 21:15) — wisdom promised, not exemption.
“they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake” (Act 6:10) — fulfilled in Stephen, who also died.
“I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings, and will not be ashamed” (Psa 119:46) — the duty stated.

pos: n. (Walter Mill, c. 1476–1558, aged parish priest of Lunan, the last person burned for heresy in Scotland, at St Andrews in April 1558)
etymology: Scots Mill, a form of Milne, from the mill; also written Myln and Mylne.
biblical_def: Walter Mill was an old man — past eighty by some accounts — who had been parish priest of Lunan in Angus, had travelled in Germany, and had married, which was itself proof of his convictions. Condemned by Archbishop Hamilton at St Andrews, he was so frail that he had to be helped to the place of judgment, and the people expected him to be inaudible; Foxe and Knox both record that his voice carried and that he answered the charges firmly, telling his judges he would not recant and that his death would be the beginning rather than the end. No burgh officer could be found willing to supply the rope and barrels, and the townspeople refused to sell them, so the archbishop's own servants provided the pyre. He was the last Scottish martyr; within eighteen months the Reformation carried the country. Joh 12:24 is the law he appealed to: “Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.” Exo 1:12 states the same providence — “the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a martyr as one who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel; and seed, figuratively, as the principle of production.
webster_full: M'ARTYR, n. One who, by his death, bears witness to the truth of the gospel.
SEED, n. The substance, animal or vegetable, which nature prepares for the reproduction and conservation of the species.
4. First principle; original; as the seeds of virtue or vice.
scriptures: Verily, verily, I say unto you, Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone: but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.
Exo 1:12
But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew. And they were grieved because of the children of Israel.
Act 8:4
Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.
Surely he shall not be moved for ever: the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance.
corruption_summary: The last martyr burned in Scotland was an octogenarian whose executioners could not buy a rope in the town, and the kingdom turned within two years.
corruption_paragraphs: Mill's death is the clearest instance in the British Isles of the principle Joh 12:24 states: the grain that dies brings forth much fruit. The refusal of the St Andrews townsmen to supply the materials was itself the signal — the population had already moved, and the hierarchy was burning a man it could no longer frighten anyone with. Act 8:4 gives the mechanism in Acts: persecution scattered the believers and “they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word,” so that suppression propagated what it meant to stop.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is the right and limited use of the maxim that the blood of the martyrs is seed. It is a statement about God's providence, not a strategy, and it must never become a reason to court death or to treat suffering as a technique. Mill did not seek the fire; he declined to lie. Psa 112:6 is the promise for such men — “the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” — and Exo 1:12 the pattern God has repeatedly chosen, multiplying His people under affliction.

“the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew” (Exo 1:12) — the providence repeated.
“they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word” (Act 8:4) — suppression propagating the gospel.

pos: n. (Alexander Alesius, 1500–1565, Scottish theologian converted by Patrick Hamilton's death, exile and professor at Frankfurt and Leipzig, who argued for the vernacular Scripture against the Scottish bishops)
etymology: Latinized from Scots Alane or Aless; he took the name Alesius from Greek alētēs, a wanderer, after his exile.
biblical_def: Alexander Alesius was a canon of St Andrews set to argue Patrick Hamilton out of his opinions, and was converted instead by watching him die. Imprisoned, he escaped to the Continent in 1532 and never safely returned. His first published work answered an edict of the Scottish bishops forbidding the laity to possess the Scriptures in the vernacular; his argument is that the Word was given to the church and not to the clergy, that the people are commanded to search it, and that a bishop who locks it up has usurped what God gave. He taught at Cambridge for a time under Cromwell's patronage, then at Frankfurt an der Oder and Leipzig, wrote commentaries, and kept up a long correspondence with the Scottish reformers from abroad. Joh 20:31 is his ground: “these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.” Rom 15:4 says “whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning,” and 2Pe 1:19 calls Scripture “a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place.”
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the vernacular as belonging to the country of one's birth; native; as, English is our vernacular language.
webster_full: VERNAC'ULAR, a. Native; belonging to the country of one's birth; as, English is our vernacular language.
EX'ILE, n. The state of being banished from one's country.
2. The person banished, or expelled from his country by authority.
scriptures: But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.
Rom 15:4
For whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope.
We have also a more sure word of prophecy; whereunto ye do well that ye take heed, as unto a light that shineth in a dark place, until the day dawn, and the day star arise in your hearts:
Psa 19:8
The statutes of the LORD are right, rejoicing the heart: the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes.
corruption_summary: A bishops' edict forbidding the people the Scriptures provoked the first Scottish book in their defence, and the argument it makes has never needed revising.
corruption_paragraphs: The Scottish prohibition of 1533 is the plainest form of the error: the Word is withheld lest the laity misread it. Alesius's answer is that Scripture itself addresses the people, tells them its purpose, and commands them to search — Joh 20:31 states why it was written and to whom, and Rom 15:4 says it was written “for our learning.” The custodial argument proves too much, since the same reasoning would keep it from the clergy, who have misread it at least as often. The perspicuity of Scripture in what is necessary for salvation is a Reformation doctrine because it is a biblical one.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition; the principle to recover is that a Bible in the hand is only half of what Alesius asked for. The withholding now is practical rather than legal: households own several versions and read none, and congregations are fed summaries. 2Pe 1:19 commends the sure word as a lamp for a dark place and adds “whereunto ye do well that ye take heed” — the taking heed being the reader's part. Psa 19:8 promises what follows: “the commandment of the LORD is pure, enlightening the eyes.”

pos: n. (the Act of Six Articles, 1539, Henry VIII's statute enforcing six points of Roman doctrine on pain of death, called by Protestants the whip with six strings)
etymology: Latin articulus, a joint, a small part, hence a clause of a document; the statute's own title was an Act Abolishing Diversity in Opinions.
biblical_def: The Six Articles of 1539 fixed the limits of Henry VIII's reformation, which had broken with the pope and intended to keep the religion. The statute affirmed transubstantiation, declared communion in both kinds unnecessary for the laity, forbade priests to marry, held vows of chastity binding, allowed private masses, and required auricular confession. Denial of the first article was treason punishable by burning, with no opportunity to abjure; denial of the others was felony. Cranmer argued against it in the Lords for three days and lost, and had to send his wife abroad. Latimer and Shaxton resigned their bishoprics. Robert Barnes, John Lambert, Anne Askew and many others died under it or under the climate it created, and it stood until repealed under Edward in 1547. Scripture answers the articles directly: Heb 10:14, “by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified”; 1Co 11:26, the cup given to all who eat; and 1Ti 4:3, which names “Forbidding to marry” among the marks of a departing from the faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an article, in church affairs, as a particular clause or item of a creed or confession of faith; and an act as a statute or law made by a legislative body.
webster_full: AR'TICLE, n. A single clause in a contract, account, system of regulations, treaty, or other writing; a particular item.
2. In the church, a particular clause or item of a creed or confession of faith.
ACT, n. In law, a statute or edict of a legislative body; a decree or determination.
scriptures: For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord's death till he come.
Forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth.
As a roaring lion, and a ranging bear; so is a wicked ruler over the poor people.
corruption_summary: Henry broke with Rome and kept Rome's religion, and the Six Articles is the statute that proves a schism is not a reformation.
corruption_paragraphs: The English breach of 1534 was jurisdictional: the king replaced the pope as head of the church in England and left the doctrine standing. The Six Articles made that explicit five years later, enforcing transubstantiation and clerical celibacy by statute, with the fire for anyone who denied the first. The lesson is that a church may change its government entirely and remain unreformed, because reformation is a matter of doctrine — of what is believed about the sacrifice of Christ, the ground of justification, and the authority of Scripture. Heb 10:14 is the article the statute could not accommodate: one offering, perfected for ever.

Two of the six are worth naming for their continuing consequences. Withholding the cup from the laity denies the ordinance its own stated form, since 1Co 11:26 makes eating and drinking the showing forth of the Lord's death. Forbidding ministers to marry is named in Scripture as a doctrine of departure, 1Ti 4:3 placing “Forbidding to marry” beside commanding abstinence from meats. Pro 28:15 is the comment on the enforcement: “As a roaring lion, and a ranging bear; so is a wicked ruler over the poor people.”
